kid.question: What message opens Isaiah 40?

options.text: Prepare for a siege
Comfort God’s people
Build a new idol
Gather more weapons

kid.explanation: The opening command is to comfort Jerusalem and announce that her hard service and guilt have reached an end.

kid.question: What should be prepared in the wilderness?

options.text: A hiding place for idols
A pasture for horses
A way for the Lord
A wall around Babylon

kid.explanation: The prepared highway and leveled terrain picture readiness for the Lord’s revealed glory.

kid.question: What lasts after grass and flowers fade?

options.text: Human beauty
A ruler’s promise
A carved image
God’s word

kid.explanation: Human life is compared to fading grass, while God’s word stands forever.

kid.question: How does the Lord carry the lambs?

options.text: In His arms
On a horse
In a cart
Across a bridge

kid.explanation: The announced God is both powerful in rule and gentle toward His flock.

kid.question: How does Isaiah compare the nations to God?

options.text: Like a mountain over Him
Like a drop in a bucket
Like a flock He fears
Like stars He cannot count

kid.explanation: The measuring questions and comparison to a drop of water place nations within the scale of God’s power.

kid.question: Who makes the carved image in Isaiah’s example?

options.text: The Lord
A shepherd
A craftsperson
A prophet

kid.explanation: Isaiah contrasts the incomparable God with images made and stabilized by craftsmen.

kid.question: What does the Lord call the stars by?

options.text: Their ages
Their colors
Their sizes
Their names

kid.explanation: The Lord stretches out the heavens and names their hosts; earthly rulers wither before Him.

kid.question: What does God give to people who feel weak?

options.text: Strength
More burdens
A carved image
A secret name

kid.explanation: God answers Israel’s fear of being overlooked by affirming His unfailing understanding and power to strengthen the faint.

kid.question: Who receives new strength in Isaiah 40:31?

options.text: Those who rely on youth
Those who wait on the Lord
Those who finish the race first
Those who gather at the mountain

kid.explanation: Even youths grow weary, but those who wait on the Lord receive renewed strength.

kid.question: Who says He is with the first and the last?

options.text: A goldsmith
A foreign king
The Lord
A messenger from Zion

kid.explanation: The Lord summons the nations to judgment and identifies Himself as the one who directs generations from beginning to end.

high-school.question: Why does the message to Jerusalem sound different from a warning of judgment?

options.text: It asks Jerusalem to deny earlier wrongs
It says Babylon has become the new covenant people
It announces comfort and pardon after hardship
It praises Jerusalem for avoiding every consequence

high-school.explanation: The opening command is to comfort Jerusalem and announce that her hard service and guilt have reached an end.

high-school.question: What do raised valleys and lowered mountains communicate?

options.text: The people must reshape every landscape themselves
The Lord can appear only on level land
The old cities must be rebuilt first
Obstacles are removed for the Lord’s coming

high-school.explanation: The prepared highway and leveled terrain picture readiness for the Lord’s revealed glory.

high-school.question: What contrast does Isaiah draw between people and God’s word?

options.text: Human life is brief; God’s word endures
People are strong; God’s word is fragile
Both fade in the same season
Neither can survive hardship

high-school.explanation: Human life is compared to fading grass, while God’s word stands forever.

high-school.question: Which pair best captures the portrait of the Lord in verses 10–11?

options.text: Distant judge and silent witness
Strong ruler and gentle shepherd
Weary traveler and frightened sheep
Hidden maker and powerless king

high-school.explanation: The announced God is both powerful in rule and gentle toward His flock.

high-school.question: What is the point of asking who measured the waters and weighed the mountains?

options.text: To teach a method for surveying land
To praise the largest nation
To show the Creator exceeds human and national power
To suggest creation was a difficult accident

high-school.explanation: The measuring questions and comparison to a drop of water place nations within the scale of God’s power.

high-school.question: Why is the image’s need to be made and secured important?

options.text: The image is too expensive for ordinary people
Only a richer image could represent God
The craftsperson has failed to use enough gold
A dependent object cannot compare with the Creator

high-school.explanation: Isaiah contrasts the incomparable God with images made and stabilized by craftsmen.

high-school.question: Why place fading rulers beside the ordered host of heaven?

options.text: To contrast temporary earthly rank with enduring divine command
To show rulers can direct the stars
To say stars are stronger than God
To identify which ruler built the heavens

high-school.explanation: The Lord stretches out the heavens and names their hosts; earthly rulers wither before Him.

high-school.question: How does the description of the tireless Creator answer Israel’s complaint?

options.text: God is too vast to notice one people
God has both awareness and strength to help
Israel must solve the problem without Him
Only strong people deserve His attention

high-school.explanation: God answers Israel’s fear of being overlooked by affirming His unfailing understanding and power to strengthen the faint.

high-school.question: Why does Isaiah mention that even young people grow tired?

options.text: To blame young people for weak faith
To forbid running and walking
To show human vigor has limits
To say strength depends on age

high-school.explanation: Even youths grow weary, but those who wait on the Lord receive renewed strength.

high-school.question: What does the courtroom invitation in Isaiah 41 emphasize?

options.text: The nations are invited to choose a new idol
The judge needs the nations to explain creation
The first conqueror has the final word
The nations must reckon with the Lord’s action in history

high-school.explanation: The Lord summons the nations to judgment and identifies Himself as the one who directs generations from beginning to end.

expert.question: What gives the repeated command to “comfort” its force in the opening verses?

options.text: The speaker changes from prophet to foreign ruler
The people are asked to comfort God for His loss
The city has escaped any need for reconciliation
A prior period of suffering is now met by announced pardon

expert.explanation: The opening command is to comfort Jerusalem and announce that her hard service and guilt have reached an end.

expert.question: How do the road image and the claim that “all flesh” will see glory relate?

options.text: Preparation leads to a public revelation beyond one location
The road limits the revelation to those who travel it
The terrain changes replace the Lord’s arrival
The announcement is addressed only to mountain dwellers

expert.explanation: The prepared highway and leveled terrain picture readiness for the Lord’s revealed glory.

expert.question: Why is the grass comparison apt in a chapter of comfort?

options.text: It proves the comfort was intended only for farmers
It shifts confidence from fragile human power to God’s enduring promise
It makes the coming glory dependent on human longevity
It describes the permanence of Babylon’s rule

expert.explanation: Human life is compared to fading grass, while God’s word stands forever.

expert.question: What is gained by placing the ruling arm beside the arm that gathers lambs?

options.text: The shepherd image corrects a mistaken claim of divine power
The ruling arm belongs to a different speaker
Divine strength is shown as compatible with tender care
Tenderness is shown as a reward for the strongest sheep

expert.explanation: The announced God is both powerful in rule and gentle toward His flock.

expert.question: How do the measurement questions prepare for the “drop of a bucket” comparison?

options.text: They imply God needs nations to complete creation
They rank different nations by their size
They turn the passage into a lesson about weights
They establish the Creator’s scale before relativizing nations

expert.explanation: The measuring questions and comparison to a drop of water place nations within the scale of God’s power.

expert.question: What tension undercuts the proposed “likeness” of God in these verses?

options.text: People must construct and steady the object they would worship
The worth of an image changes with its materials
The question assumes every image depicts a nation
The worshipper must choose a tree that will endure

expert.explanation: Isaiah contrasts the incomparable God with images made and stabilized by craftsmen.

expert.question: What answer do verses 21–26 give to the challenge “to whom will ye liken me”?

options.text: The mightiest prince can approach God’s power
No earthly ruler or fashioned object matches the Creator who orders the heavens
The host of heaven provides a literal portrait of God
The question is settled by the quality of an image’s metal

expert.explanation: The Lord stretches out the heavens and names their hosts; earthly rulers wither before Him.

expert.question: Why place Israel’s claim that its way is hidden immediately before God’s inexhaustible understanding?

options.text: It grants the complaint and changes the subject
It shows knowledge, but not power, is the issue
The juxtaposition directly challenges the idea of divine neglect
It restricts God’s concern to the heavens

expert.explanation: God answers Israel’s fear of being overlooked by affirming His unfailing understanding and power to strengthen the faint.

expert.question: What makes “waiting” active rather than passive in the closing image?

options.text: It excuses the people from any future movement
It requires physical stillness until youth returns
It makes personal endurance independent of God
Trust in the Lord sustains renewed running and walking

expert.explanation: Even youths grow weary, but those who wait on the Lord receive renewed strength.

expert.question: How does “calling the generations from the beginning” answer the question about the rising conqueror?

options.text: It locates historical upheaval within the Lord’s enduring agency
It identifies the conqueror as the final judge
It suggests later generations must repeat the same campaign
It treats the nations’ fear as proof of their innocence

expert.explanation: The Lord summons the nations to judgment and identifies Himself as the one who directs generations from beginning to end.
